One big difference there is that all those tools augment rather than replace human labor. One person can achieve labor in the same amount of time that previously would have taken 4 humans or whatever. Autonomous systems on the other hand completely remove humans from the picture. Eventually there will be millions of taxis operating without a single driver. The whole job of 'taxi driver' in any reasonably direct form will be destroyed. Wheat harvester might have evolved into driver of wheat harvesting machine, but the job is still there in some form for plenty of humans. Taxi drivers, by contrast, will simply no longer exist in any form.

This is why the comparison between automation and things like the industrial revolution are somewhat inappropriate. We're not workers on the dawn of the industrial revolution. We're horses on the dawn of the automobile. There will certainly be new jobs that didn't exist before but in the longrun horse labor has been relegated to little more than a quaint sideshow - and the majority of human jobs will eventually follow suit. I'm just hoping that once this becomes apparent that we don't follow India's lead. Regulating against automation is a very predictable knee jerk reaction to technological progress.

I think this depends on your outlook. I would 100% agree in the long run. But in the short run the main reason that, for instance, factory jobs no longer exist is not because of outsourcing but because of automation. Automation is what makes a few hundred people able to do jobs that used to take thousands. Outsourcing is what then sends those few hundred remaining jobs to Mexico.

Getting rid of as many jobs as possible is going to be a great thing in the longrun, but people are already suffering in the interim of this transition. And that suffering is undoubtedly going to get much worse before it gets better.

The solution is retraining. We already have unemployment, medicaid, and other social safety nets. If getting paid not to work is suffering then how is getting paid and having to go to work better? If we can afford to have high paying worthless jobs then we can afford to have equally high unemployment benefits with the added bonus of free time.

Think of a simple figure - the ratio of the number of people needed to provide all goods and services for a nation. This ratio decreases thanks to increases in productivity and technology. For instance the cross-sector productivity since the 50s is up by about 250%. That means if I took 5 people to make 1 item in the 50s it would now take just 2 people do so. If we say that our ratio was 50:100 then today it would be 20:100. However, of course that's only part of the picture. While we've lost the milk men, now we have millions of programmers. As technology evolves new fields emerge and helps increase the ratio back up.

However, the important thing here though is that this ratio is undoubtedly decreasing. You can see this in most every metric in every single developed nation in the world. Labor force participation decreases, unemployment and underemployment increases. So retraining isn't a solution. And in fact I don't think there is any solution. This declining ratio is also going to play a large role in the reason that wages are stagnant to declining in most industries, or why you see "entry level" positions requiring years of experience and industry specific expertise. There's more qualified people than ever for just about everything. Adding more qualified people just exasperates the problem.

As long as there are problems in the world there are jobs to be done.
